summary: Hepatitis refers to inflammation of the liver parenchyma. While it can be caused by toxins, alcohol, or autoimmune processes, viral hepatitis (Types A, B, C, D, and E) is a leading cause of global morbidity and mortality.

sections.p: Hepatitis refers to inflammation of the liver parenchyma. While it can be caused by toxins, alcohol, or autoimmune processes, viral hepatitis (Types A, B, C, D, and E) is a leading cause of global morbidity and mortality.

b: Hepatitis A & E: Transmitted via the fecal-oral route. They typically cause acute, self-limiting illness and do not lead to chronic carrier states.
Hepatitis B (HBV): A unique DNA virus (Hepadnaviridae) transmitted parenterally, sexually, or perinatally. It can lead to chronic infection, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma.
Hepatitis C (HCV): An RNA virus primarily transmitted via blood-to-blood contact. It has a high rate of chronicity.
Hepatitis D (HDV): An incomplete virus that requires the presence of HBsAg (HBV) to replicate.
Prodromal Phase: Malaise, anorexia, nausea, and right upper quadrant pain.
Icteric Phase: Jaundice, dark urine (bilirubinuria), and pale stools.
Laboratory Findings: Marked elevation of transaminases (ALT and AST), elevated bilirubin, and specific serological markers (e.g., HBsAg, Anti-HAV IgM).
Vaccination: Effective vaccines exist for HBV (included in the pentavalent vaccine) and HAV. HBV vaccine is freeze-sensitive and requires careful cold chain management.
Screening: Essential in antenatal care to prevent vertical transmission and in blood transfusion services to ensure blood safety.
Drug-Induced Hepatitis: Certain medications, notably Rifampicin and Isoniazid, are known to cause hepatotoxicity, requiring monitoring during treatment.
Fulminant hepatic failure characterized by altered consciousness (encephalopathy) and flapping tremors (asterixis).
Signs of coagulopathy such as easy bruising, mucosal bleeding, or prolonged oozing from injection sites.
Deepening jaundice, ascites, and peripheral edema indicating severe loss of liver synthetic function.
Development of hepatocellular carcinoma or cirrhosis in chronic viral hepatitis cases.

sections.p: Management focuses on identifying the specific etiology, providing supportive care to allow the liver to recover, and utilizing targeted therapy for chronic or severe cases.
b: Supportive care includes adequate hydration, high-calorie nutrition, and avoidance of alcohol or hepatotoxic substances.
Nucleoside analogues like Tenofovir or Entecavir for chronic Hepatitis B to suppress viral replication and prevent cirrhosis.
Direct-acting antivirals for Hepatitis C to achieve a sustained virologic response and eradicate the virus.
Corticosteroids or Azathioprine for autoimmune hepatitis to dampen the immune-mediated destruction of hepatocytes.
Refer to a gastroenterologist if there is evidence of acute liver failure, cirrhosis, or diagnostic uncertainty.
Serial monitoring of liver enzymes and viral load to assess treatment response and disease progression.
Universal vaccination for Hepatitis A and B for all infants and high-risk groups.
Screening of household and sexual contacts to prevent further transmission of blood-borne viruses.
Regular ultrasound and Alpha-fetoprotein monitoring for patients with cirrhosis to screen for early liver cancer.
Drug-induced liver injury (DILI) often mimics viral hepatitis; a detailed drug history including herbal supplements is essential.
Biliary obstruction can cause jaundice and elevated transaminases, but typically presents with significant alkaline phosphatase elevation and dilated ducts on ultrasound.
Wilson’s Disease may present as acute hepatitis in younger patients, often distinguished by low ceruloplasmin and Kayser-Fleischer rings.
Aminotransferase levels do not always correlate with the severity of liver necrosis or long-term prognosis.
In end-stage cirrhosis, ALT and AST may appear 'normal' due to the lack of remaining viable hepatocytes to release enzymes.
A positive Hepatitis C antibody test does not distinguish between an active infection and a previously cleared infection; HCV RNA is required.

whenToSeekHelp: Development of altered consciousness, confusion, or flapping tremors (asterixis).
Rapidly worsening jaundice or dark tea-colored urine.
Persistent vomiting with an inability to maintain oral hydration.
Severe abdominal pain or signs of gastrointestinal hemorrhage.
Evidence of easy bruising or spontaneous bleeding from gums or mucosa.

faq.q: What defines the window period in Hepatitis B testing?
faq.a: The time between the disappearance of HBsAg and the appearance of Anti-HBs, where IgM Anti-HBc may be the only marker of acute infection.

faq.q: Which types of viral hepatitis are transmitted via the fecal-oral route?
faq.a: Hepatitis A and E are primarily transmitted through contaminated food and water, whereas B, C, and D are blood-borne.

faq.q: Why is Hepatitis D unique among the viral hepatitides?
faq.a: It is a defective virus that requires the presence of Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) to replicate and cause infection.

exam: Interpret a serological profile showing HBsAg negative, Anti-HBc positive, and Anti-HBs positive.
List three extra-hepatic manifestations of chronic Hepatitis C infection.
Discuss the criteria used to differentiate between acute liver injury and fulminant hepatic failure.
